## Database architecture, data sources, and quality control

Every method described in this chapter, and every result in Chapter
4, is built on top of a single relational database
(`database/geochem_operational.sqlite`) rather than a collection of
spreadsheets. This was a deliberate choice: this project draws on more
than a dozen independent data sources with incompatible formats,
units, and naming conventions, and keeping them in one queryable
schema is what makes it possible to ask a question like "what is the
chloride-to-boron ratio of every real thermal sample from 1950 to
2026" as a single reproducible query rather than a manual
spreadsheet-merging exercise repeated every time the question is
asked slightly differently.

**Data sources.** The database is populated from field sampling
(chemistry, isotopes, and temperature at the Lower Sinter Terrace
wells and springs); the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection
(NDEP), both a bulk historical chemistry export and public-records-
request compliance documents for Ormat's production wells; the Nevada
Division of Water Resources (NDWR), which supplies well construction
logs and water-rights records; the Nevada Division of Minerals (NDOM),
which supplies the official state permit record for every Ormat well
(permit number, API number, well type, and status); the U.S.
Geological Survey, for streamflow, water level, and historical
specific-conductance time series; NOAA, for weather and, most recently,
hourly barometric pressure; the Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology's
statewide geothermal-well compilation; and a set of historical
literature sources -- principally Sorey and Colvard [@sorey1992],
Mariner and Janik [@mariner1995], and Skalbeck [@skalbeck2001] -- whose
own tables of dated chemistry, well completions, and subsurface depth
points have been transcribed and ingested directly rather than merely
cited.

**Pipeline design.** Each source has its own ingestion script under
`scripts/ingest/`, and every script follows the same two rules: it is
idempotent (re-running it against a database that already has its
data does not create duplicates), and it never silently overwrites a
value that is already on file. New, less-certain information (for
example, a well identity inferred from a scanned drilling report, or a
station name that does not exactly match anything already in the
database) is staged into a review table and only promoted into the
core schema once a human has confirmed it -- a pattern used throughout
for exactly the situations where guessing would be easy but wrong.
`scripts/run_pipeline.R` orchestrates the full set of ingestion and
analysis stages and reports, stage by stage, what ran, what was
skipped, and how long each step took.

**Quality control.** Several real, substantive data-quality problems
were found and fixed over the course of building this database, and
they are worth naming because they materially affect how much the
results in Chapter 4 can be trusted. A missing alkalinity parameter
in the NDEP chemistry feed meant charge-balance error initially looked
like roughly 60% for most samples; once alkalinity was correctly
mapped and unit-converted, the median charge-balance error for the
same samples dropped to about 0.7%, with the majority now passing the
standard plus-or-minus 5% quality threshold. Several analytes (silica,
arsenic, boron, iron, manganese) were found stored in mixed units
(micrograms and milligrams per liter) within the same column and are
now converted consistently before use. A systematic elevation-unit
error (feet stored as if they were meters) was found and corrected
project-wide. A join-correctness bug in the code that pairs chemistry
samples with the nearest streamflow reading silently returned a
0-minute time difference for every match for years before it was
caught; fixing it revealed that only a small, specific subset of
samples actually overlap the U.S. Geological Survey's live discharge
record closely enough to be paired at all, which is itself an
important, previously-hidden limitation on Chapter 4's discharge
calculation. A standing, automated quality-control pass
(`scripts/qc/qc_data_integrity_checks.R`) checks for missing data,
implausible values, PHREEQC convergence failures, and near-duplicate
locations on every pipeline run, and its results are summarized in a
standing status report rather than checked only when something looks
wrong.

## Field methods

**Spring and well remapping.** Ormat's own records list several
springs at the Lower Sinter Terrace as inactive; a central field task
of this thesis is walking that terrace and confirming, for each one,
whether it is in fact dry, seeping, or actively discharging, and
recording its condition with a GPS-tagged field photograph and
observation. This same photo-to-location pipeline is used for every
field visit, not just the terrace survey: a photograph's embedded GPS
and timestamp, where present, can register a new monitoring location
or check an existing one's coordinate without a coordinate ever being
typed in by hand.

**Chemistry and isotope sampling.** Water samples are collected at
springs, wells, and creek stations, with field measurements (pH,
temperature, specific conductance) taken at the time of collection and
laboratory analyses (major ions, alkalinity, trace elements, and
delta-18-O/delta-D isotopes) run afterward. Chapter 6 lays out, in
detail, the calibration-sampling plan this thesis proposes for the
year ahead.

**Temperature logger network.** Continuous temperature loggers are
deployed at springs, wells, and along the eruption fissure itself,
recording at a regular interval since deployment began in 2025. These
loggers are the most direct way to see whether the 2025 eruption's
thermal signature has been stable, cooling, or shifting laterally
since it was capped, without needing a person physically present at
the vent.

**Conductivity loggers as a chloride proxy.** Two continuous specific-
conductance loggers were deployed in Steamboat Creek on July 15, 2026: one
co-located with the existing U.S. Geological Survey gauge near Rhodes
Road (SBRR, serving as the upstream/control site) and one further
downstream near Geiger Grade (SBGG, the downstream site), matching the
same two site roles Sorey and Spielman used for their own chloride-
flux calculations [@sorey2008; @sorey2017]. The premise, following
the same method already demonstrated at Yellowstone [@mccleskey2012;
@mccleskey2016], is that specific conductance should track chloride
(and other conservative geothermal solutes) closely enough to serve
as a continuous, inexpensive proxy for a quantity that is otherwise
only obtainable from discrete, lab-analyzed samples. Establishing that
relationship for the first time at Steamboat, with a real calibration
dataset, is this thesis's second central objective, and is the
subject of the sampling plan below and in Chapter 6.

## Proposed chloride sampling plan (condensed)

A full, reproducible statistical analysis behind this plan is given in
`notebooks/09_sampling_campaign_design.qmd`, and a complete
decision-facing version, including cost-benefit tiers and candidate
additional sites, is given in Chapter 6. In brief: because no real
chloride sample yet overlaps the period the conductivity loggers have
been running, the single highest-priority field task is a short (two
to four week), daily-to-sub-daily intensive chloride-sampling campaign
at both SBRR and SBGG -- and since the loggers have already been
running since mid-July 2026, this window is now planned to start as soon as
possible (this fall/winter) rather than waiting for a conventional
spring/summer field season. Following that intensive window, chloride
sampling should continue at roughly monthly intervals for a full
annual cycle -- not just the remainder of one field season -- so the
calibration can be tested against winter baseflow, spring runoff,
summer, and fall conditions before being treated as final, with
additional samples deliberately timed around large storms and spring
snowmelt, when the relationship is most likely to break down. A Monte
Carlo subsampling analysis on the existing conductivity record
(Chapter 4) supports the underlying sampling-frequency logic
quantitatively: reconstructing the mean specific conductance from
daily sampling gives about 3-4% error, while weekly sampling costs
about 7-8% (after removing the days the loggers sat in open air), with the error growing smoothly rather than showing a sharp
cliff at any particular interval -- though that analysis still only
has a roughly twelve-week, summer-to-early-fall record to draw on, which a full year of
monthly sampling is specifically meant to extend. Every calibration
sample should also carry major-ion and, for a subset, isotope
chemistry, since chloride alone cannot distinguish simple mixing from
evaporative concentration.

This thesis explicitly proposes a chloride sampling campaign at the two
existing conductivity-logger stations, **SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream
control) and SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream)**, the only two points where
a chloride measurement can be paired directly with a continuous
conductance record. @tbl-samplingplan lays out the design.

| Site | What is sampled | Frequency / timing | Why |
|------------------|----------------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream control) | Chloride, major ions (Na, K, Ca, Mg, SO4, alkalinity), field pH/temperature/specific conductance | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks (intensive window, starting fall/winter 2026) | Establishes the calibration's short-timescale behavior and noise floor against the logger's continuous record. |
| SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream) | Same analyte set as SBRR | Daily to sub-daily for 2-4 weeks, concurrent with SBRR | A second, independently calibrated site tests whether one relationship serves the whole system or each site needs its own equation. |
| SBRR and SBGG | Same analyte set | Monthly for a full annual cycle after the intensive window | Tests seasonal stability across winter baseflow, spring runoff, summer baseflow, and fall transition. |
| SBRR and SBGG (opportunistic) | Same analyte set | Additional samples around large storms and spring snowmelt | These are the conditions most likely to break conservative mixing (dilution, flashy runoff). |
| SBRR and SBGG (subset) | delta-18-O / delta-D isotopes | Roughly one isotope sample per season, with a regular chloride visit | Chloride alone cannot distinguish thermal/meteoric mixing from evaporative concentration; isotopes can. |

: Proposed chloride sampling plan at the two conductivity-logger stations. {#tbl-samplingplan}

**Calibration models and validation.** Three forms are fit and compared,
each for a stated reason: a linear regression of chloride on specific
conductance (with temperature if it improves fit), the simplest form and
the one used for conductance-as-chloride-proxy work in Yellowstone
[@mccleskey2012; @mccleskey2016]; a log-linear fit, because chloride is
strictly positive and spans over an order of magnitude across site types;
and a generalized additive model fit with `mgcv` [@wood2017], which lets
the relationship curve where the data demand it. A random forest fit with
`ranger` [@breiman2001] serves only as a benchmark for how much skill a
flexible model can extract from the same predictors. Because chloride and
conductance are autocorrelated time series, models are validated with
rolling-origin (blocked, time-aware) cross-validation [@bergmeir2012],
which trains only on earlier data and tests on later data, and are scored
by cross-validated root-mean-square error rather than an in-sample fit.

## Statistical methods

A range of standard, appropriately-chosen statistical methods is used
throughout this work rather than a single default test applied
everywhere. Two-sample comparisons use Welch's t-test where normality
is reasonable and Kruskal-Wallis with pairwise Wilcoxon rank tests
where it is not; multivariate ion relationships are explored with a
significance-tested Pearson correlation matrix and principal component
analysis; hydrochemical facies are identified by hierarchical (Ward)
clustering and cross-checked against an independent Gaussian-mixture
fit and k-means; linear mixed-effects models account for repeated
sampling of the same well or location rather than pooling all
observations as if independent; and nonparametric bootstrap confidence
intervals are used where a real sample size is too small to trust a
classical interval. Full statistical reporting -- test statistic,
effect size, confidence interval, and assumption checks -- for every
real test run against this project's data is given in
`notebooks/07_historical_context_sorey1992.qmd` and
`notebooks/08_statistical_synthesis.qmd`, paired with the exact code
that produced each result.

## PHREEQC and geochemical modeling methods

Chapter 2 gives the full background on charge balance, saturation
index, the five thermodynamic databases used and why, and the two
geothermometry approaches this project relies on. In brief, aqueous
speciation and saturation-index modeling is run through the real
PHREEQC 3 executable [@phreeqc] against every sample with complete
enough chemistry to support it (233 real samples as of this writing),
with a database auto-selected per sample by temperature and total
dissolved solids and a documented fallback when the first choice fails
to converge. A real two-end-member conservative-mixing model has also been
completed, using chemically distinct, not merely spatially close,
end-members, following the modeling principle laid out at the end of
Chapter 2. Two real PHREEQC inverse-modeling runs have also been
attempted; both report zero feasible models (one of them only after a
real parser bug -- fixed 2026-10-25 -- was found to have reported a
false positive for the first attempt). The rest of this section describes the
actual workflow -- which samples get modeled, how their chemistry is
assembled and cleaned up before PHREEQC ever sees it, and what the
output is actually used to decide -- rather than re-deriving the
equations and database choices already given in Chapter 2.

**Sample eligibility.** Not every sample in the database gets run
through PHREEQC. A sample qualifies once it has pH, temperature, and
major-ion concentrations for chloride, sodium, potassium, calcium,
magnesium, and alkalinity -- the minimum set a real speciation
calculation needs, not just whatever happens to be on hand. Field-
measured pH and temperature are preferred over laboratory-reported
values when both exist, since a lab reading taken days after
collection has already drifted from in-situ conditions; lab values are
used only when no field measurement exists. Additional analytes --
silica, sulfate, lithium, boron, and a handful of trace metals -- are
pulled in when available but aren't themselves gatekeeping. Samples
that don't clear this bar aren't silently dropped, either: each is
logged with the specific field it's missing, so the real, and
currently still substantial, gap between how many samples exist and
how many are PHREEQC-ready stays visible instead of disappearing into
an unexplained smaller number.

**Assembling and cleaning the chemistry first.** Samples come from
several sources spanning more than seventy years -- field sampling,
NDEP's routine and public-records-request chemistry, and historical
literature (Sorey and Colvard, Mariner and Janik, and Skalbeck)
transcribed directly rather than merely cited -- and those sources
don't agree on units or on how alkalinity is reported. Every
concentration is standardized to mg/L before it reaches a SOLUTION
block, and any alkalinity value reported on a CaCO3 basis is converted
to this project's standard HCO3-mass-equivalent basis using the real
50.05/61.02 equivalent-weight ratio (a conversion factor of 1.2189).
Getting this right turned out to matter more than it sounds like it
should: an earlier version of this pipeline simply left alkalinity out
for one major chemistry source, which alone pushed median charge-
balance error from a real ~0.7% up to a misleadingly bad ~60% for the
exact same samples -- a data-handling artifact, not an actual
analytical problem, and a good reminder to check a "bad" charge
balance before assuming the chemistry itself is at fault.

**End-member grouping.** Samples with complete chemistry are assigned
to one of three groups -- a thermal end-member (outlet and thermal-well
samples), mixed waters (chemistry carrying a partial but real thermal
signature), and dilute background waters -- using the hydrochemical-
facies clustering described above, cross-checked against PHREEQC's own
fluid-type classification rather than just asserted from the site-type
label on file. This is what makes the conservative-tracer check below,
and the Chapter 4 Cl/B comparison, real chemically-defined groups
rather than an arbitrary site-based split.

**Conservative-tracer evaluation.** Four ratios -- Cl/B, Na/Cl, Li/Cl,
and SiO2/Cl -- are tracked across every era of chemistry on file (the
1950s, the 1990s, and the present) specifically to ask whether the real
thermal end-member's composition has stayed stable over seven decades,
independent of whatever a chloride-conductance calibration eventually
finds. A ratio that drifts meaningfully through time, or differs
systematically between eras, is treated as real evidence about
source-fluid stability -- see Chapter 4's Cl/B result -- rather than
folded quietly into one pooled average that would hide exactly that
question.

**Mixing and inverse modeling.** A two-end-member conservative-mixing
fraction is computed directly from chloride, then used to build a real
PHREEQC `MIX` block combining the two end-member solutions at that
fraction and comparing PHREEQC's own predicted speciation against the
sample's observed chemistry -- a genuine test of the mixing hypothesis,
not just an arithmetic ratio. `INVERSE_MODELING` goes further, solving
for mixing fractions and mineral mass transfer simultaneously, within
stated elemental uncertainty bounds. In the interest of being upfront
about where this actually stands: one real mixing run and two real
inverse-modeling runs exist as of this writing, and both inverse runs
report zero feasible models. The first used a representative rather
than a time-paired thermal/meteoric end-member pair (sample 816/829),
because no two chloride samples have yet been collected close enough
together in time to serve as a genuinely paired end-member set --
exactly the gap the calibration sampling plan above is meant to
close; it was originally reported as having found one feasible
solution, but a parser bug (fixed 2026-10-25) turned out to have
misread PHREEQC's own echoed-back input composition as a found
solution, when PHREEQC's own raw output actually says "Number of
models found: 0." The second, gas-informed run (Chapter 4) also finds
zero feasible models, this time from real post-mortem residuals
exceeding the stated uncertainty bound, not a parser artifact. The
automated parser's own remaining real gap -- it has never correctly
extracted a solution's mineral-mass-transfer numbers from PHREEQC's
raw text output -- is moot for both real runs on file, since neither
found a feasible solution to extract numbers from.

**Interpretation framework.** Every PHREEQC run in this project is
ultimately answering one of three questions, not run just because the
chemistry happened to be complete enough to try: are the real water
types here chemically distinct from each other, is conductance
behaving conservatively enough to stand in for chloride, and has the
thermal end-member's own composition held up over the full
seventy-year record. A modeling result that doesn't actually bear on
one of those three questions isn't reported here just because it's
available.


**Forward reaction-path titration.** Given that real inverse-modeling
attempts against the Lower Sinter Terrace flowpath consistently find
zero feasible solutions, a complementary forward method was built: mix
two named end-members at a known (stored or freshly computed)
conservative fraction with a PHREEQC `MIX` block, then use a PHREEQC
`REACTION` block to explicitly step one or more candidate mineral
phases' mass transfer, in both directions (net precipitation and net
dissolution), and compare the resulting modeled trajectory against the
target sample's own real chemistry at each step. This turns an open-
ended search into a direct, visualizable question: does some specific,
physically named amount of mineral dissolution or precipitation
reconcile the model with reality, and if so, how much. The method was
also used to test two concrete hypotheses against a sample (SBS_0001)
whose own chemistry -- the highest sulfate and lowest alkalinity of its
peer group -- pointed toward a non-carbonate explanation: adding
sulfate or fluoride mineral phases as additional candidates, and
substituting a different, higher-sulfate meteoric end-member in place
of the standard one.

**Assumptions and limitations of the forward titration method.** Four
are stated here plainly, since they bear directly on how much weight
the results above can carry. First, every candidate phase supplied to a
given run is titrated by the identical reaction-progress amount at each
step -- there is no real constraint, chemical or otherwise, that the
system actually dissolves or precipitates two phases in a one-to-one
ratio; a result is only as good as that simplifying choice. Second, a
single mixing fraction is held fixed for the whole titration, computed
once from chloride before the reaction is explored -- the two are not
jointly fit, so a real sample whose best explanation actually involves
*both* a different mixing fraction and reaction could be mis-scored
under this method. Third, the fit metric compares PHREEQC's modeled
values directly against reported lab concentrations with no allowance
for analytical uncertainty; a sample within ordinary analytical error
of the model looks exactly as "wrong" as one with a real, geologically
meaningful discrepancy. Fourth, and demonstrated concretely rather than
just asserted, results are conditional on which candidate phases are
supplied at all: the sensitivity test run against SBS_0001 (Chapter 4)
shows the same target's best-fit error ranging from 44.5 percent down
to 30.6 percent depending on phase and end-member choices alone, with
no single choice fully resolving the underlying tension. SBRR's own
status as a conservative, not theoretically pure, meteoric reference
(stated above) compounds all four points, since every one of these
tests inherits that same starting assumption.

**Geothermometer equilibrium checks.** Two Giggenbach ternary diagrams
(Na-K-square-root-Mg maturity, and Cl-SO4-HCO3 water-source), plus a
multicomponent mineral-equilibration diagram (Reed and Spycher 1984,
using the already-stored PHREEQC temperature-sweep output), test
whether the Na/K geothermometer is trustworthy here and whether any
candidate mineral set converges on a single shared equilibration
temperature, rather than relying on the quartz/chalcedony pair alone.
No new PHREEQC execution is needed for any of the three.

## Fissure gas geochemistry

Three real free-gas samples collected April 2026 at the Lower Sinter
Terrace fissure by T. Fischer and K. Mtili (UCSB), with P. Ruprecht,
give this project its first gas-chemistry dataset. One sample (NV26-2)
carries a flagged contamination risk -- a possible Giggenbach-bottle
leak, at a point where sampling broke through fresh asphalt -- and is
treated accordingly, not silently averaged with the other two. Every
sample is first corrected for atmospheric entrainment (measured O2
assumed entirely atmospheric; air-derived N2 estimated from the dry-air
N2/O2 ratio of 3.773 and subtracted) before the D'Amore-Panichi
[@damore1980] multicomponent gas geothermometer already described
above is run on the corrected composition, and compared against the
only other Steamboat-specific gas chemistry on file, Mariner & Janik's
[-@mariner1995] 1991-1994 well-23-5 analyses (see
`scripts/analysis/gas_air_correction.R` and
`scripts/analysis/gas_historical_comparison.R`).


## A gas-informed parent-fluid reconstruction and flowpath trace

NV26-1's gas composition, paired with the fissure water sample, is
used to work backward toward a pre-boiling "parent" fluid: a Giggenbach
sodium/potassium reservoir temperature (quartz/chalcedony sit below
measured temperature here, so are not used for this step), a standard
single-step adiabatic steam-loss fraction from a saturated-steam-table
enthalpy balance, conservative-species concentrations scaled back by
(1 minus that fraction), and a PHREEQC `GAS_PHASE` re-equilibration
with the real, air-corrected gas composition at the reservoir's own
saturation pressure. The same method is applied, diagnostically, to
the resort-tank sample using the same gas composition (no gas sample
exists at the tank itself) -- but the well feeding the resort tank is
pumped with a true, intermittent air-lift pump, a forced-aeration
mechanism this method's steam-loss physics does not represent, so its
reconstruction is reported but not treated as a reliable estimate of a
deep fluid; the resort tank's as-measured (as-pumped) chemistry is
used instead everywhere it appears as a target or end-member. The
fissure's reconstructed parent fluid, the as-measured discharge at
every node (including the resort tank), a nearby well, and this
project's two Steamboat Creek chloride-mass-balance stations are
assembled into one real flowpath table spanning chemistry, PHREEQC
saturation indices, geothermometry, and stable isotopes. Every run's
thermodynamic database, charge-balance error, and convergence status
are logged explicitly
(`data/derived/phreeqc/parent_fluid_diagnostics.csv`), including one
real, reported convergence failure (see Results).
## The thermal layer, point positions, and the resort budget: methods

**Data and method.** The thermal map used here is a georeferenced layout export
of the 2025 survey (O. Callahan, NBMG, unpublished imagery), in NAD83 / UTM zone 11N
(EPSG:26911), 16,907 by 4,477 pixels at about 0.17 by 0.10 m. A semi-transparent
temperature layer lies over a hillshade, with analyst annotations (yellow ellipses
and 13.5 m circles, outlines) drawn into the pixels. Each pixel was matched to the
nearest color of the 7-44 degree Celsius ramp in the calibrated legend (the TIFF has
no legend of its own, so the same stretch is assumed), keeping pixels within a fixed
color distance of the ramp and excluding the annotation colors. The mask was closed
over about 0.5 m, because the layer is speckled at pixel scale, and polygonized into
the database table `Thermal_Areas`. The ramp saturates at 44 degrees Celsius.

**Sources.** Polygons are assigned to a source using the annotation outlines. A polygon inside an ellipse takes the source that ellipse marks (fissure zone, Lower Terrace channel, creek-corridor springs and seeps, the streak at the pipe end, or the hillside ellipse); a polygon outside every outline and within 60 m of the resort tank logger is resort infrastructure; polygons inside the 13.5 m circles are kept separate. Area is polygon area, and temperature is the area-weighted mean of the pixel temperatures.

**Positions and aliases.** Points are overlaid in one coordinate system (EPSG:26911). A position is changed only after the author reviews the imagery and the ArcGIS layers, through a corrections table that records the old and new coordinate, the source, the uncertainty and the reason, and that is re-applied each time the database is rebuilt. Historical White and Collar feature names are attached as aliases when a project point lies within 10 m of the historical feature's digitized position; records are not merged.

**Budgets.** Surface heat loss is summed over the polygons as

$$q = h\,(T_s - T_a) + \varepsilon\sigma\,(T_s^4 - T_a^4),$$

with the convective coefficient $h$ = 10, 15 and 25 W/m^2^/K, emissivity $\varepsilon$ = 0.95, ambient $T_a$ = 10 C, and $T_s$ the polygon's mean temperature (the ramp saturates at 44 C, so this is a lower bound). The heat carried by the thermal inflow is $Q\rho c\,(T_{th} - T_{creek})$ with $Q$ = 58.65 L/s from the chloride balance and $c$ = 4.18 kJ/kg/K. The creek energy balance uses $Q_{in} = Q_{down} - Q_{up}$ and $Q_{in}T_{in} = Q_{down}T_{down} - Q_{up}T_{up}$, and the thermal-water temperature is $T_{th} = [Q_{in}T_{in} - (Q_{in} - Q_{th})T_{nt}]/Q_{th}$ with the non-thermal inflow $T_{nt}$ = 10-20 C. The resort share of the thermal inflow is

$$\text{share} = \frac{Q_r\,C_r}{F_{down} - F_{up}},$$

with $C_r$ = 849 mg/L the resort tank chloride and $F$ the chloride fluxes at SBBV and SBRR (g/s).

**Resort schedule.** Logger A009 in the resort tank is analyzed in local time, using readings above 68 C and days with at least 90 percent coverage: time of the daily minimum, daily range, the share of the day at the plateau, and the warming-or-plateau fraction (the share of hourly steps in which the hourly mean changes by more than -0.02 C). Weekdays and weekends are compared with Wilcoxon tests. To test whether the resort cycle appears in the creek, the hourly conductance difference between SBGG and SBRR (UTC timestamps converted to local time, daily mean removed) is correlated with the tank temperature, both as 24 hourly means and as lagged hourly series.

## The sampling plan in depth: calibration pairs, the Monte Carlo design, and Lower Terrace mapping

Sampling serves three purposes in this thesis, and the plan is built so that one visit serves all three: pairing chloride with conductance for the calibration (RQ1), setting how often chloride must be measured (RQ2), and characterizing the discharge points of the Lower Sinter Terrace so that the thermal map can be tied to chemistry (RQ3 and RQ4).

**What the Monte Carlo test establishes, and what it does not.** The test draws 200 random start days for each candidate interval, subsamples the real conductance record at that interval, interpolates between the samples, and compares the reconstruction with the full record (the procedure is given above). @tbl-mcsummary gives the result with air-exposure days removed. Daily and every-other-day sampling reconstruct the record to within about 3-5 percent of its mean; weekly sampling to 7-8 percent, with a worst case near 10 percent; biweekly sampling to 9-10 percent, with a worst case of 12-13 percent. The test covers the concentration signal only, not mass flux, because no discharge record overlaps the loggers, and it is a statement about conductance, not chloride, until the calibration pairs exist. The daily swing in conductance is only 9-12 uS/cm at either station, so time of day matters little for the schedule. The test will be re-run on chloride once paired samples exist, and with discharge once a discharge series overlaps the loggers.

| Sampling interval | SBRR mean (%) | SBRR 95th percentile (%) | SBGG mean (%) | SBGG 95th percentile (%) |
|-----------------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Daily | 3.6 | 4.0 | 3.1 | 5.0 |
| Every other day | 4.3 | 4.8 | 4.1 | 5.0 |
| Weekly | 6.9 | 7.7 | 7.8 | 9.8 |
| Biweekly | 9.5 | 12.1 | 8.5 | 13.2 |

: Reconstruction error of the conductance record as a percent of its mean, over 200 random campaigns per interval, with air-exposure days removed. {#tbl-mcsummary}

**Calibration pairs.** The design is an intensive daily-to-sub-daily window followed by monthly sampling across a full annual cycle (@tbl-samplingplan). A reasoned minimum is 15-20 pairs for a stable regression and 30-40 for a seasonally defensible one, and a tier of about 40 analyses is recommended for a one-person thesis. This is a reasoned count, not a power analysis, because no real chloride-conductance pairs exist yet to compute one against. Pairing chloride with the major ions lets the mixing model be checked in the same samples, and about one isotope sample per season at the two creek stations is the only way to separate evaporation from conservative mixing.

**Mapping the Lower Terrace.** @tbl-lstsampling lists proposed sampling by source, with the sources taken from the thermal map. The counts are a starting point to be fitted to the laboratory budget and to site access, and they come in addition to the roughly 40 calibration analyses.

| Source (from the thermal map) | Why | Proposed samples per year | Measurements |
|-------------------|-----------------------|---------------|---------------------|
| Fissure zone (SBF_0001, SBF_0002, NV26-1) | Deep-source end-member; gas repeat | 4 water (quarterly), 2 gas | Major ions, boron, lithium, silica, 2 isotope samples; gas composition |
| Lower Terrace channel (largest anomaly, 161 m^2^) | Whether it shares the fissure's source | 4 (quarterly), access permitting | Major ions, silica, field temperature, pH, conductance |
| Creek-corridor springs and seeps (17 polygons; SBS_0001, SBS_0002, SBS_0006; springs 45, 46, 44e and 50n by alias) | Diffuse thermal inflow to the creek | 12 (6 springs, 2 seasons) | Chloride, major ions, field parameters |
| Resort tank and overflow, with the creek above and below the entry point | Resort share of the thermal inflow | 12 (4 dates, 3 points) | Chloride, conductance, temperature, flow |
| Capped eruption pipe (SBW_0003), if accessible | The 2025 eruption pipe | 2 | Major ions, temperature, water level |

: Proposed Lower Terrace sampling by source, in addition to the calibration analyses. {#tbl-lstsampling}

**Repeat thermal surveys.** The 488 m^2^ at or above 30 degrees Celsius is a baseline. If NBMG can repeat the calibrated drone flights each season, the same pixel-to-polygon method gives a change metric (area by source and season) at no laboratory cost, and a repeat of the October 2025 flight would show whether the creek-corridor springs and the fissure zone are growing, shrinking or moving.

**Decision rules.** After the first full cycle, residuals are compared by season and site type. A single calibration is kept only if its error is acceptable against a threshold set explicitly with the committee (the recommendation script takes the threshold as an input and has no default); otherwise site-specific equations are reported with their uncertainty, as RQ1's deliverable states.

## Proposed extension: a Leapfrog geologic model to inform mixing pathways and reaction paths

Rachel Micander's proposal builds a 3-D structural model in Leapfrog and ArcGIS from well collars, directional surveys, mud logs, well chips, borehole-image logs and geophysical products, to show fluid pathways, structure and the distribution of sinter and other rock below the surface. This proposal borrows that workflow at a smaller scope and for a different purpose. The model is not meant to explain structure or to simulate flow. It gives the chemistry a geometry.

**What the model would do.** It has four jobs. First, compartments: grouping samples by lithology and fault block, so that end-members and mixing pairs are chosen within and across compartments on stated geologic grounds. Second, pathways: giving path lengths and orientations for the 1-D mixing models along the fissure-to-creek flowpath, so that mixing fraction can be plotted against distance. Third, reaction paths: showing which rock the water meets (altered alluvium, volcanics, altered granodiorite, sinter), so that the phases supplied to the PHREEQC reaction-path titration are chosen from the geology and not by trial; the calcium-alkalinity tension at SBS_0001, which no simple phase set resolved, is the open question this targets. Fourth, a check on the chemistry: comparing the principal components of the PHREEQC output by compartment.

**Data on hand.** Collars, depths and elevations for 110 wells (elevations from the 1 m DEM unless a permit or survey value exists); 140 lithology intervals from the NBMG permit compilation and 158 from the 27 well logs in Collar's thesis (86 linked to wells); Skalbeck's cross-sections and 241 point depths to the units Qal, Tv, AltKgdpKm and Kgd; 9 faults, 53 fissure traces and the sinter-terrace outline; and the thermal polygons. All are exported in UTM zone 11N with Z from the DEM. The limits are that every hole is treated as vertical except 83C-6ST1, which has a deviation survey, that lithology quality varies, and that no permeability data exist.

**Workflow.** The database is exported to Leapfrog (fault network, lithologic units, intersections with the wells); compartment labels are written back to the database; the PHREEQC and mixing runs are grouped by compartment; the principal-component analysis is repeated by compartment. The fault traces digitized in ArcGIS are the main dependency, and nine are on file.

**A principal-component analysis of the PHREEQC output.** @fig-phreeqc-pca shows a first version: 381 samples and 17 variables (log activities of the major ions, saturation indices of calcite, aragonite, dolomite, gypsum, anhydrite, halite, quartz and chalcedony, pH and ionic strength). The first component, 49.5 percent of the variance, is salinity: ionic strength, sodium, chloride, sulfate and the halite and gypsum saturation indices. It separates the creek waters from the thermal-influenced wells and outlets. The second, 28.1 percent, is pH and carbonate saturation. The analysis will be repeated with the Leapfrog compartment as the grouping variable and on the terrace flowpath alone.

```{r fig-phreeqc-pca}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Principal components of the PHREEQC speciation output for 381 samples (17 variables), colored by the database's site type, with variable loadings. The first component is salinity and the second is pH and carbonate saturation."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of two principal components with creek samples to the left and well and outlet samples to the right, and arrows for ionic strength, sodium, chloride, pH and carbonate saturation indices."
```

## Resistivity, collaborators, and data access

**Resistivity.** Christopher Kratt (UNR geophysicist) may be able to run electrical-resistivity lines across the fissure zone, the terrace and the creek if the property owners give permission. Resistivity would add what chemistry and logs cannot: the extent of a conductive, clay-altered cap, the depth of the fissure zone, and the lateral extent of saline water between wells, which would give the Leapfrog model fault and cap geometry in the gaps. White and others carried out resistivity surveys at Steamboat in the 1960s [@white1964b], so the method has precedent at this site. Two lines are proposed as a first step: one across the fissure zone and the Low Terrace Fault, and one along the creek corridor through the resort. Whether this happens depends on access, equipment and schedule, so it is not a deliverable of this proposal.

**Historical Lower Terrace information and logs.** Phil Busick and Gene Savoy hold much of the history of the Lower Sinter Terrace properties. The requests to them are: records and any drilling or construction information for the capped eruption pipe (ten candidate identities are on file); well logs and permits for the resort and spa wells, including NDWR log 26097; water-right and pumping information for the resort well; their observations of when springs and fissures changed; and access for sampling, for a field measurement of the capped pipe, for a walk of the resort overflow, and for any geophysics. Rachel Micander and NBMG hold the 2022-2025 timeline and field observations.

**Ormat.** Following the list in Rachel Micander's proposal (well collars, directional surveys, mud logs, borehole-image logs and geophysical products), a request to Ormat would be limited to what bears on the Lower Terrace: Lower Steamboat production and injection well logs, water levels and pressures. Any release would need an agreement, and nothing in this proposal depends on it.

**Public records.** NDEP (UIC permits, U230 field forms and chemistry; a request for deeper-well water levels is pending), NDOM (permitted-well records) and NDWR (well logs; the resort's water-right records have not yet been retrieved).
## Geologic and hydraulic context: explicitly out of scope beyond what already exists

Beyond the bounded Leapfrog model proposed above, three further steps -- a digitized fault geometry, a full
three-dimensional Leapfrog geologic model built on top of it, and a
MODFLOW groundwater-flow model built on top of that -- would eventually
let this project's chemistry be tested against real subsurface
structure and real flow paths, rather than inferred from chemistry and
proximity alone. None of the three is pursued as an active deliverable
of this thesis, for the same reason in each case: each needs a real
input this project does not yet have, and building any of them without
that real input would produce a model dominated by untested assumptions
rather than real constraints -- exactly the outcome the batch-modeling
limitation discussed in Chapter 2 is meant to avoid, not just defer
elsewhere.

Digitized fault traces need a committed ArcGIS georeferencing session
against the fault-and-lineament map published by Collar and Huntley
[@collar1990] (chosen because it also locates several wells already
resolved in this database, giving natural control points); an ingestion
script (`ingest_fault_traces.R`) is already built and waiting for that
real input. A calibrated hydraulic-conductivity and storage-coefficient
field needs real pump-test drawdown data, which does not yet exist for
any Lower Sinter Terrace well (an Aqtesolv analysis of such data, once
collected, is a concrete near-term opportunity given the author's own
ongoing groundwater hydrology coursework, but is not assumed here on
any fixed timeline). The only real, site-area transmissivity/storage-
coefficient values on file today are literature reference points, not a
calibrated field: four dated aquifer tests summarized by Sorey and
Colvard [-@sorey1992] (roughly 1,250-9,500 square feet per day) and one
point from Collar and Huntley [-@collar1990] for spring 42w
(approximately 3,000 square feet per day).

What already exists and is genuinely usable today, at essentially no
further cost: real well collar, total-depth, and completion-interval
data for roughly half the wells on file, already exported in Leapfrog's
own input format and standing ready the moment real fault geometry
exists to build on top of it; and a standing NDEP data request for
deeper-well water levels (only two or three wells inside the Steamboat
field itself currently carry continuous, current water-level data) that
would, if it comes through, support a real, field-specific
potentiometric surface. Both are named as concrete next steps for
whoever picks this thread up next, not as deliverables of this
proposal.
